intro: Lazur is an AI assistant for supply chain planners on Mac. Hold a key, ask a question, and it sees your screen, points at the cell that broke and answers out loud. This page covers where planners' hours go, a realistic working day, and where Lazur helps and where it does not.
tldr: Surveys put planner-adjacent work in hours. One 2024 survey reports nearly 14 hours a week tracking data, and a 2023 survey reports 27 hours a week modelling scenarios.
Most of that work happens in Excel, Google Sheets and email. Lazur works in whatever Mac app is on screen.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about the sheet in front of you. Lazur points at cells, explains formulas and answers out loud.
Lazur drafts supplier emails and dictates notes with hold fn. It does not click buttons, edit files or change your plan.
Check your employer's data rules before you show supplier prices or customer forecasts to any AI tool.

blocks.text: Supply chain planning is a job of gaps. A planner matches demand with supply, watches for shortages and chases the people who can close them. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics groups this kind of work under logisticians. Its handbook says these workers forecast and align product demand and supply flows, monitor product risk and act as liaison with suppliers or customers. BLS lists 255,100 logisticians in 2025, with projected growth of 18% from 2025 to 2035. The handbook does not mention spreadsheets. Your week will, though. BLS is the closest official category, not a perfect match for your title, so use these numbers as context.
Where a supply chain planner's hours go

Start with the numbers, and read them carefully. LeanDNA, working with Wakefield Research, surveyed 250 supply chain, inventory and planning executives. Its March 2024 release says supply chain professionals spend nearly 14 hours a week manually tracking data. That is almost two full workdays. The release does not say which data counts, or how the figure was calculated. Treat it as a signal from leaders, not a timesheet for planners. If you want a real number for your team, time your own data tracking for a normal week.

Board International's 2023 planning survey adds a second number. Its article says planners average 27 hours a week modelling business scenarios. The same article says 98% of decision-makers do some planning in spreadsheets like Excel. That 98% covers decision-makers in general, not supply chain planners alone. The article also gives two sample sizes, 2,450 in one section and 2,400 in another. It does not say how much of the 27 hours happens in a spreadsheet. Scenario work is real. The split between tools is still unclear.

Email takes its share of the week too. Microsoft's 2023 Work Trend Index surveyed 31,000 full-time workers across 31 markets. Its WorkLab page says the heaviest 25% of email users spend 8.8 hours a week on email. The same page says the average employee spends 57% of their time communicating in meetings, email and chat. These figures describe heavy email users and the wider workforce, not planners. They are also from 2023, so treat them as a rough guide to inbox load.

blocks.text: Put the three figures side by side and the pattern is clear. Tracking data, modelling scenarios and handling email each take hours a week. None of these studies measures a planner's full week. If you pitch a tool or a process change, size the problem with your own calendar and your own tracker. Outside numbers help you ask the question. They cannot answer it for your team.
Why the spreadsheet becomes the bottleneck

LeanDNA's release adds a sharper point. It reports that 76% of executives do not have a predictive view of supply and demand. It also says 92% make gut decisions at least sometimes, because their reports lack predictive guidance. Put simply, many teams spend hours gathering data and still lack a clear view of what comes next. Leaders ask what will happen. Often the planner gets the question, and the spreadsheet only shows what already happened.

That gap splits your work into three jobs. The first is pulling and checking data. The second is explaining why a number moved. The third is writing to a supplier, a sales lead or a manager about it. Lazur helps most with the second and third. It can also speed up the first when the data is already on screen. It does not replace the data owner, and it cannot confirm a receipt date for you.
Excel for supply chain planners on Mac: what Lazur does

Keep the sheet open and hold ⌥ ⌘. Lazur sees your screen while you hold the keys, so it can read the rows and columns in view. Ask where a column is. It circles the column and adds a label, then tells you what it is. Ask why a formula returns an error. It explains the references in plain language, one at a time. It does not type the fix. When you ask how to do something, Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click.

Version matters when a menu looks different. Microsoft's release notes list Excel for Mac 16.114.3, dated 27 Oct 2026, with only quality and performance improvements. The last build with a UI change in those notes was 16.113, on 16 Sep 2026. That update added chat history to Copilot in Excel, reached from a menu icon in the upper-left corner of the Copilot pane. If a guide does not match your screen, check your build under Excel > About Excel first, then compare it with the release notes.

blocks.title: Select first
blocks.text: Click the cell you care about, then hold ⌥ ⌘. Lazur reads what is on screen, so bring the row and its headers into view before you ask.
A worked example: a shortage that appears late

Say the weekly supply plan shows one SKU row in red. Projected on hand dips below zero in a single week, then climbs back the week after. Your first question is usually why. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur to point at the red cell. It can circle the Projected on hand column and explain which inputs feed that cell, if the formulas are visible. Then you check the receipt date with the supplier and decide what to do about the gap.

Do not accept the explanation without a test. Trace the row by hand, from opening stock to the closing balance. If your sheet disagrees with the planning system, the system of record usually wins. Ask the data owner which number is right. Lazur can help you word that question. It cannot see your ERP, so it only knows what is on your screen.
Outlook and Slack: cut the back and forth

Supplier threads are where planners lose time to rewriting. Ask Lazur to draft a reply that names the part, the quantity and the date you need. Choose the tone you want, short and firm or warm and brief. Read the draft before you send. Lazur drafts and types text. You decide what leaves your outbox.

Use hold fn for longer replies. Dictation types clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app, including Outlook and Slack. A personal dictionary helps with SKU codes and supplier names, so the spelling comes out right. Snippets hold standard lines, such as your cutoff times. Clipboard slots keep a supplier reference handy while you switch windows.

Check your Outlook version before you follow an older guide. Microsoft's Outlook for Mac support page says to try the new experience, then turn off the Legacy Outlook switch. To switch back, open Help > Revert to Legacy Outlook. The same page says support for legacy Outlook for Mac would end in October 2026, depending on your license. That month has passed. Expect menus to differ from older screenshots. For repeat filing, read [how to create a rule in Outlook on Mac](/how-to/create-a-rule-in-outlook) instead of sorting by hand.
Everyday tasks: reminders, calendar and notes

Not every planner task lives in a spreadsheet. Ask Lazur to set a reminder to call the carrier after lunch. Ask what is on your calendar for the S&OP review, then ask it to add a follow-up event. Timers, Apple Reminders, Calendar events, notes, music and volume all work by voice. If your events live in Outlook, see [how to create a calendar event in Outlook on Mac](/how-to/create-a-calendar-event-in-outlook). These small jobs add up when you move between a sheet, a mailbox and a planning tool.
Research for carrier and supplier facts

Some questions need public sources. Ask Lazur to research a carrier's published cutoff times or a customs rule for your lane. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, through the Lazur for Chrome extension. When it finishes, Lazur returns a summary and a report. Open the sources yourself before a fact enters a plan. Public pages change, and your signed contract still governs the terms.
What Lazur will not do

items: It does not click buttons or operate other apps for you.
It does not edit your workbook, your ERP or your planning tool.
It is not a plugin or add-in for Excel, Outlook or any planning suite.
It has no partnership with any app maker.
It runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.

blocks.text: Privacy and your employer's data rules

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer your question. They are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Those statements describe how the product handles data. They do not decide what your company allows.

Planning data often includes supplier prices, contract terms and customer forecasts. Some employers limit which AI tools can see that kind of data. Follow your employer's rules, and ask IT or your data owner if you are unsure. This page does not claim any compliance certification for Lazur, and you should not assume one exists.

blocks.title: Check before you hold the keys
blocks.text: Holding ⌥ ⌘ on a sheet sends what is on screen to AI providers to answer. If that sheet shows supplier pricing or customer forecasts, check your company's data rules first.
Mistakes planners make with AI help

items: Trusting the first answer. Test any formula explanation on a single row before you change the plan.
Asking for a number with no source. Ask Lazur where a figure comes from, then open that source yourself.
Reading the copy, not the system. The planning system or ERP usually holds the record that counts.
Holding the keys on the wrong window. Bring the right sheet forward, then ask.
Sending a draft unread. Lazur drafts. You approve every word that goes to a supplier.

blocks.text: Excel or Google Sheets: which one fits your week

Some teams keep heavy models in Excel and share tracking in Google Sheets. Pick the tool your team already uses, then learn its quirks. For Excel, read [Excel for supply chain planners on Mac](/for/supply-chain-planners/excel). It covers MRP math, Power Query limits and voice help. For a shared sheet, read [Google Sheets for supply chain planners on Mac](/for/supply-chain-planners/google-sheets). If a shared list needs a filter, see [how to add a filter in Google Sheets on Mac](/how-to/add-a-filter-to-a-range-in-google-sheets).
Planning suites like SAP IBP

Many planners also work in a dedicated planning suite. I could not confirm whether SAP's Excel add-in runs on a Mac, because the SAP help pages would not open while I checked. Lazur works with what is on screen, but it is not a plugin for those tools, and it does not connect to them. Check the vendor's Mac support before you plan around a workflow.
A first week with Lazur on your Mac

items: Download Lazur for Mac from the [download page](/download). A free trial starts when you first open the app, and it needs no credit card.
Open a sheet you use every week. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask what a red cell means.
Hold fn in Outlook or Slack and dictate one short reply. Check the spelling of your supplier names.
Ask for one reminder and one calendar event. Confirm the time afterward.
Read the [pricing page](/pricing) before you decide to pay for anything.

blocks.text: Keep the first week small. Pick one sheet, one email thread and one recurring meeting. Note where the minutes went. After a week you will know which jobs Lazur helps with and which still need your own judgment.

faq.question: Is Lazur an AI assistant for supply chain planners that works inside Excel?
faq.answer: Lazur works in any Mac app that is on screen. It is not a plugin or add-in, so it does not run inside Excel. Hold ⌥ ⌘ while the sheet is open and it can point at cells, explain formulas and answer out loud. It does not edit the workbook.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with SAP IBP, Kinaxis or other planning tools?
faq.answer: Lazur works with whatever is on your screen, but I did not verify any planning suite. Check the vendor's Mac support first. Lazur is not a plugin for those tools and does not connect to them.

faq.question: Can Lazur change my forecast or submit an order?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps. When you ask how to do something, it guides you one click at a time and waits for each click. It drafts text for you to review before anything is sent.

faq.question: Is my supplier data safe with Lazur?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your employer's data rules still apply, so check them before you hold the keys.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Windows is planned, not available. Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs.

faq.question: Which Excel version should I check before I follow a guide?
faq.answer: Check your build under Excel > About Excel. Microsoft's release notes list Excel for Mac 16.114.3 on 27 Oct 2026, with only quality and performance improvements. Older guides may show menus from earlier builds.

faq.question: Can Lazur help with Google Sheets too?
faq.answer: Yes, when the sheet is open in Chrome or another browser on your screen, Lazur can point at cells and explain formulas. Research runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension. Lazur does not edit the sheet for you.

painPoints.title: Scenario work runs in spreadsheets

painPoints.title: Email never stops
painPoints.text: Microsoft's 2023 data puts the heaviest 25% of email users at 8.8 hours a week. Supplier chasers, internal asks and calendar invites stack up through the day.

painPoints.title: Leaders want the next few weeks
painPoints.text: LeanDNA reports 76% of executives lack a predictive view of supply and demand. Planners often explain the past when leaders ask what comes next.

painPoints.title: Constant switching between tools
painPoints.text: A planner moves between a sheet, a mailbox, a planning system and a chat thread in the same hour. Each switch costs attention, and most teams never measure it.
